brightness: Infected cells are a little darker on average (about 163 vs 168 out of 255). Parasites are stained dark purple on the slide, so a stained blob inside the cell pulls the average brightness down. The effect is moderate (d = -0.56): the two curves overlap a lot, so brightness alone would misclassify many cells.
saturation: Infected cells are more strongly coloured (0.25 vs 0.20). The stain that makes the parasite visible adds purple/pink colour, while healthy cells stay a paler, more even pink. Colour is one of the cues the network can use, but again the overlap is large (d = 0.53).
texture: This is the strongest single feature (d = 0.72). Infected cells have more contrast inside them (17.2 vs 15.5) because a dark parasite sits against paler cell material, while an uninfected cell is more uniform. It tells us the model should focus on patterns inside the cell, not on the cell outline.
cell_area: Infected and uninfected cells fill almost the same share of the image (72% vs 73%, d = -0.21). That is reassuring: the model cannot cheat by judging cell size, so it has to learn from the cell's content.
image_pixels: Raw image dimensions are nearly identical between classes (d = 0.13). Good news for validity: if image size predicted the label, a model could score well for the wrong reason (a shortcut). Here it can't, so resizing everything to 128x128 loses no hidden label information. Every individual feature overlaps heavily between classes, which is why a CNN that combines many subtle patterns beats any single measurement (95.8% test accuracy).
